questions.q: What does the psalmist say Yahweh’s discipline feels like to him?
questions.a: He says he feels as though Yahweh had shot arrows into him and his hand had struck him.

questions.q: What does the psalmist ask Yahweh not to do?
questions.a: He asks Yahweh not to rebuke him in his anger and not to punish him in his wrath.

questions.q: Why does the psalmist say his whole body is sick?
questions.a: His whole body is sick because of Yahweh’s anger, and there is no peace in his bones because of his sin.

questions.q: How does the psalmist describe his iniquities?
questions.a: He says his iniquities overwhelm him and are a burden too heavy for him to bear.

questions.q: What has happened to the psalmist’s wounds?
questions.a: His wounds are infected and smell because of his foolish sins.

questions.q: How does the psalmist describe his daily condition?
questions.a: He is stooped over and humiliated every day, and he goes about mourning all day long.

questions.q: What fills the psalmist within?
questions.a: He is filled with burning from within, and there is no health in his flesh.

questions.q: How does the psalmist describe the extent of his suffering?
questions.a: He is numb and utterly crushed, and he groans because of the anguish of his heart.

questions.q: What does the psalmist say the Lord knows about him?
questions.a: The Lord understands his heart’s deepest yearnings, and his groanings are not hidden from the Lord.

questions.q: What three things does the psalmist say are happening to him physically?
questions.a: His heart is pounding, his strength is fading, and his eyesight is dimming.

questions.q: How do the psalmist’s friends and neighbors respond to his condition?
questions.a: His friends and loved ones shun him because of his condition, and his relatives stand far away.

questions.q: What do those who seek the psalmist’s life do to him?
questions.a: They lay snares for him and speak destructive and deceitful words against him all day long.

questions.q: How does the psalmist respond to those who seek to harm him?
questions.a: He acts like a deaf man who hears nothing and a mute man who says nothing in reply.

questions.q: In whom does the psalmist place his hope?
questions.a: He waits for Yahweh and trusts that the Lord his God will answer him.

questions.q: What does the psalmist fear will happen if his foot slips?
questions.a: He fears his enemies will rejoice and gloat over him.

questions.q: What two things does the psalmist say about his current situation?
questions.a: He says he is about to stumble and that he is in constant pain.

questions.q: What does the psalmist confess to Yahweh?
questions.a: He confesses his guilt and says he is troubled about his sin.

questions.q: How do the psalmist’s enemies treat him?
questions.a: His enemies are numerous, hate him without cause, repay him evil for good, and accuse him even though he has pursued what is good.

questions.q: How do his enemies repay the good he has done?
questions.a: They repay David evil for good and they hurl accusations at him.

questions.q: What names does David use when he asks Yahweh for help?
questions.a: He calls him, “Yahweh”, “God”, “Lord”, and “my salvation.”

questions.q: What does the psalmist ask Yahweh not to do?
questions.a: He asks Yahweh not to abandon him and not to stay far away from him.

questions.q: What does the psalmist ask Yahweh to do?
questions.a: He asks Yahweh to come quickly to help him.

commentary.text: Verses 1–11 Nothing will disquiet the heart of a good man so much as the sense of God's anger. The way to keep the heart quiet, is to keep ourselves in the love of God. But a sense of guilt is too heavy to bear; and would sink men into despair and ruin, unless removed by the pardoning mercy of God. If there were not sin in our souls, there would be no pain in our bones, no illness in our bodies. The guilt of sin is a burden to the whole creation, which groans under it. It will be a burden to the sinners themselves, when they are heavy-laden under it, or a burden of ruin, when it sinks them to hell. When we perceive our true condition, the Good Physician will be valued, sought, and obeyed. Yet many let their wounds rankle, because they delay to go to their merciful Friend. When, at any time, we are distempered in our bodies, we ought to remember how God has been dishonoured in and by our bodies. The groanings which cannot be uttered, are not hid from Him that searches the heart, and knows the mind of the Spirit. David, in his troubles, was a type of Christ in his agonies, of Christ on his cross, suffering and deserted.

Wicked men hate goodness, even when they benefit by it. David, in the complaints he makes of his enemies, seems to refer to Christ. But our enemies do us real mischief only when they drive us from God and our duty. The true believer's trouble will be made useful; he will learn to wait for his God, and will not seek relief from the world or himself. The less we notice the unkindness and injuries that are done us, the more we consult the quiet of our own minds. David's troubles were the chastisement and the consequence of his transgressions, whilst Christ suffered for our sins and ours only. What right can a sinner have to yield to impatience or anger, when mercifully corrected for his sins? David was very sensible of the present workings of corruption in him. Good men, by setting their sorrow continually before them, have been ready to fall; but by setting God always before them, they have kept their standing. If we are truly penitent for sin, that will make us patient under affliction. Nothing goes nearer to the heart of a believer when in affliction, than to be under the apprehension of God's deserting him; nor does any thing come more feelingly from his heart than this prayer, “Be not far from me.” The Lord will hasten to help those who trust in him as their salvation.
